record_type_quote: Experiment 1 was a direct replication of Pechmann and Zerbst (2002 ; Experiment 4).

targets.title: The activation of word class information during speech production
targets.evidence_quote: We did this by attempting a direct replication of one of the findings of Pechmann and Zerbst (2002 , Experiment 4).
targets.outcome_quote: Experiment 1, a replication of Pechmann and Zerbst (2002 , Experiment 4), revealed a word class effect in the sentence frame condition (replicating Pechmann & Zerbst) and in the bare noun naming condition (contra Pechmann & Zerbst), suggesting that the word class effect could potentially reflect an imageability effect.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors explicitly compare the tested word class effects to this original; outcome follows the reported agreement and disagreement.

targets.authors: Pechmann, T.; Garrett, M. F.; Zerbst, D.
targets.title: The time course of recovery for grammatical class information during lexical processing for syntactic construction
targets.evidence_quote: If the word class effect observed here and by Pechmann and colleagues (2004 ; Pechmann & Zerbst, 2002 ) does not reflect a lexical effect, it would remove such evidence as support for models that assume word class constraints on lexical selection (e.g., Dell et al., 2008 ). In Experiment 2, we tried to establish whether a word class effect could be obtained when the variable imageability was controlled.
targets.outcome_quote: Experiment 2 revealed that the word class effect could not be separated from the imageability effect: Naming latencies were sensitive to distractor imageability (see Lupker, 1979 ), but were not sensitive to distractor word class when imageability was controlled. These results conflict with the results of Pechmann and colleagues (2004 ; Pechmann & Zerbst, 2002 ).
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors explicitly compare the tested word class effects to this original; outcome follows the reported agreement and disagreement.

reasoning: Full author manuscript, including references, verified by title, DOI and all five authors. Experiment 1 directly repeats the 2002 experiment; Experiment 2 tests the word class effect attributed to both 2002 and 2004 with imageability controlled. Other lexical studies are background comparisons, not targets. The 2002 comparison contains explicit agreement and disagreement; the 2004 comparison is an explicit conflict.
